[Member 2] · payload, affiliate model, victims and negotiation (slides 6 to 9)
[Member 3] · law enforcement, recommendations and conclusions (slides 10 to 12)

slides.speaker: Member 1
slides.text: Hi, we're presenting our investigation of the RansomHub ransomware campaign. I'm [Member 1], and I'll cover our question, the context, our method and the attack lifecycle. [Member 2] will cover the payload, the affiliate model, the victims and the negotiations. [Member 3] will finish with law enforcement, our recommendations and our conclusions. Our headline is on the slide: RansomHub grew because its rivals were taken down, and it collapsed without any police action against it.

slides.speaker: Member 1
slides.text: Our question has two parts. First, how did RansomHub's affiliates actually break in, extort and negotiate? Second, did any law-enforcement action degrade the operation, or did the affiliates simply move to other brands? Our evidence is one fully logged intrusion from November 2024 plus eighteen public sources. We used the Diamond Model and the kill chain for the intrusion, and a before-and-after comparison for each law-enforcement action.

slides.speaker: Member 1
slides.text: Here's the context. In December 2023 the FBI disrupted ALPHV, and in February 2024 Operation Cronos hit LockBit. RansomHub launched between the two and recruited their stranded affiliates. By August 2024 the FBI and CISA counted at least 210 victims, the largest count of any ransomware brand that year, and they published a joint advisory. In April 2025 its infrastructure went dark.

slides.speaker: Member 1
slides.text: To see how the affiliates worked, we modelled one intrusion that The DFIR Report documented from the victim's own logs. The adversary was an unnamed affiliate working from a virtual machine. Its capabilities were password spraying, Mimikatz, two remote-management tools and Rclone. The infrastructure was a handful of IP addresses for spraying, logging in and stealing data. The victim was an organisation with remote desktop exposed to the internet. We chose this case because every stage is in the logs. What we can't see is who the affiliate was or what ransom was demanded.

slides.speaker: Member 1
slides.text: The timeline is the most useful finding for defenders. The password spray worked on day one, and the attacker immediately dumped domain credentials. Day two brought network scans and a remote-management tool on the backup servers. On day three they copied out just over two gigabytes. They came back through Splashtop on day five and encrypted on day six, 118 hours after first logging in. Each item on the right was a chance to stop this. I'll hand over to [Member 2] for the payload.

slides.speaker: Member 2
slides.text: Thanks. I'm [Member 2]. Before encrypting, the RansomHub encryptor takes away every route to recovery. It stops virtual machines and about thirty processes, deletes shadow copies, and clears the event logs. Only then does it encrypt, using a separate key pair for each victim. It won't run without a password, it encrypts large files in chunks so it finishes fast, and the operators built their own tool, EDRKillShifter, to switch off security software first.

slides.speaker: Member 2
slides.text: The money explains why affiliates joined. They kept ninety percent of every ransom, and it went straight into their own wallet. That mattered because ALPHV had just kept a twenty-two million dollar payment from its own affiliate. The operators also set rules: no targets in the former Soviet states, no attacking a victim twice after payment, and from June 2024 a five-thousand-dollar deposit to join.

slides.speaker: Member 2
slides.text: The victim list looks random by sector, and we think it is. Change Healthcare, Frontier, Christie's and Kawasaki Europe are four different industries. What they share is exposure: remote desktop on the internet, or an unpatched edge device like a Citrix or Fortinet box. Across 210 victims the FBI counted eleven critical-infrastructure sectors. The only firm exclusion was geography.

slides.speaker: Member 2
slides.text: Negotiation data is scarce. Only one of 295 public ransomware chats is RansomHub's, because each victim got a private chat run by the affiliate. Incident-response firm Arete gives us the medians from its 2024 cases: a nine-hundred-thousand-dollar opening demand and a three-hundred-and-fifty-thousand-dollar payment, so payers settled at about thirty-nine percent. The public cases show the pressure tactics. RansomHub claimed half a million Christie's clients; Christie's notified about forty-six thousand. Kawasaki and Frontier both got countdown clocks. Over to [Member 3].

slides.speaker: Member 3
slides.text: Thanks. I'm [Member 3]. This table answers the second half of our question. The ALPHV and LockBit takedowns supplied RansomHub's affiliates. The joint advisory published its tools, but our November case used exactly those tools. Charges against a Scattered Spider member, a documented RansomHub affiliate, came in September 2025, after RansomHub had already gone dark. Nothing reached the core operators, and the affiliates moved to DragonForce and Qilin. One limitation: nobody has confirmed why RansomHub collapsed, so a sealed investigation can't be ruled out.

slides.speaker: Member 3
slides.text: So, four things to do, each tied to a finding. Detect the long middle of the attack: password spraying followed by a successful remote-desktop logon, credential replication from a machine that isn't a domain controller, and Rclone on port 443. In a response, assume data was stolen before encryption and check the attacker's claims against your own logs. Take remote desktop off the internet and patch edge devices. And keep offline backups and a payment policy agreed in advance.

slides.speaker: Member 3
slides.text: To conclude: RansomHub was a brand wrapped around a mobile workforce of affiliates. Takedowns of its rivals built it, and market pressure ended it. For defenders, the window is the six days before encryption, when every stage left a trace. And because the same playbook now runs under DragonForce and Qilin, track the affiliates and their tradecraft rather than the brand name. We'd welcome your questions and feedback.
